newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: YEAREND - S.African shares set for brighter 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - S.African shares set for brighter 1997.

text.p: South African shares may be flat early in 1997, weighed down by a sluggish economy, but fair earnings growth and improving confidence should lift prices in the second half, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

A poll of 11 equity strategists, conducted towards the close of a choppy year on the South African bourse, found stocks were expected to appreciate more than 15 percent in 1997 after a meagre seven percent this year.

"It's going to be a slow start but by year-end things should start to kick up here -- that's based on world economies," said David Shapiro, joint managing director of brokerage Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
Analysts said the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) would also be helped by a slowdown in the rand's fall and an expected boost to sentiment as the government's economic reforms start to kick in.
Steady gains were expected to continue into 1998, but becoming more subdued in the latter half of the year as the country braced itself for the 1999 national elections.

The poll showed the JSE's all-share 100 percent index, which charts all shares excluding pyramid companies, debentures and preference shares, ending the 1997 year at a consensus 7,711 -- a 15.7 percent increase on Tuesday's closing level of 6,666.4.
Forecasts ranged between a high of 8,400 and a low of 6,800.
The industrial index was seen reaching 8,789 from 7,897.4, with the range 8,000-9,350.
For end-1998, estimates for the all-share index fell in a 10,400-8,296 band with the consensus at 9,238.

Analysts said the rand, which has lost almost 30 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar this year and kept foreign investors shy of South African equities, was set to register only modest losses in 1997.

A recent Reuter poll of 28 economists forecast an exchange rate for the rand of 4.92 against the dollar by the end of 1997, and 5.17 by the end of the following year. The rand closed Tuesday at 4.6840 bid to the dollar.
Analysts said Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's macro-economic strategy, a five-year programme unveiled in June which aims to boost economic growth and jobs, should start showing results by late 1997.

"If we are not there (around the 8,200 level on the all-share index) by the end of the year, then we're in trouble. Then it means that none of South Africa's economic plans are working," Shapiro said.
The government document predicts gross domestic product will grow by 2.9 percent in 1997 and 3.8 the following year.
But economists polled last month were less optimistic, forecasting growth of only 2.2 percent in 1997 and 3.15 in 1998.

That downbeat outlook, coupled with punitively high interest rates, will keep a brake on the market in 1997, leading to an effective derating despite nominal price rises, according to Denzil Newman, portfolio manager Syfrets Managed Assets.
"We see 1997 earnings growth up by 15 to 20 percent but I would expect something of a derating so we would put this market up only between 10 and 15 percent next year," he said.

Looking forward to 1998, Richard Jesse, a director of Fleming Martin Securities said nervousness may hamper the stock market later in that year ahead of the election in April 1999 when President Nelson Mandela has said he will step down.
"There might be a bit of a slowdown as the market discounts the succession, and possible violence," he said.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
